candidates.statement: This guidance incorporates updates to the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (FD&C Act) as 25 amended by section 3630 of the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2023 and will replace the final 26 guidance for industry and review staff of the same title issued in June 2018 when finalized. 27 Changes from the final guidance include updates to reflect revised statutory text that makes the 28 provisions in section 502(a) of the FD&C Act (21 U.S.C. 352(a)) regarding communication of 29 HCEI to payors applicable to devices. This guidance also includes updates to align its 30 recommendations with the new section 502(gg) of the FD&C Act, which provides that “no drug 31 or device shall be deemed to be misbranded” under section 502(f)(1) (21 U.S.C. 352(f)(1)) 32 because of certain truthful and not misleading information provided to payors. HCEI and product information provided by firms to payors about their medical products must be 73 truthful and not misleading. 12 This guidance provides FDA’s recommendations for firms to help 74 them ensure that their communication of HCEI to payors about approved/cleared medical 75 products is truthful and not misleading. Specifically, section III.A of this guidance provides 76 FDA’s thinking on frequently asked questions regarding communication of HCEI to payors 77 about approved/cleared medical products under section 502(a) of the FD&C Act (21 U.S.C. 78 352(a)). FDA considers firms’ communications of HCEI to payors that otherwise meet the 79 definition under section 201(m) of the FD&C Act (21 U.S.C. 321(m)) to be labeling. 13
candidates.context: Payors are a sophisticated audience with a range of expertise in multiple disciplines, as well as 62 established procedures for carefully considering evidence about medical products. Generally, 63 payors possess the financial resources and motivation to closely scrutinize information about 64 medical products as part of their decision-making process, including an evaluation of the 65 limitations and reliability of that information. Payors seek a range of information on the 66 effectiveness, safety, and cost-effectiveness of approved/cleared medical products, including 67 information from firms, to help support their product selection, formulary management, and/or 68 coverage and reimbursement decisions on a population basis. Often, this information differs 69 from — and can be provided in addition to — the information FDA reviews in making 70 approval/clearance decisions. 71 12 See secti

candidates.statement: 13 The first sentence of section 502(a)(1) of the FD&C Act provides that a “drug or device” is deemed to be misbranded “[i]f its labeling is false or misleading in any particular.” Under longstanding FDA practice and FDA’s statutes, regulations, and case law, “labeling” encompasses more than merely the label of the drug but extends to other written, printed, or graphic matter “accompanying such article” (section 201(m) of the FD&C Act; see also 21 CFR 1.3(a)). According to Kordel v. United States , 335 U.S. 345, 350 (1948), the language “accompanying such article” in the labeling definition in the FD&C Act includes materials that supplement or explain an article; “[n]o physical attachment one to the other is necessary. candidates.statement: FDA recognizes that in certain instances, there can be tension between the public health interests 105 directly advanced by the premarket review requirements and other important interests. For 106 example, as previously discussed, FDA recognizes that in some situations, payors need to plan 107 for and make coverage and reimbursement decisions for medical products and uses far in 108 advance of the effective date of such decisions. In making decisions on a population basis, 109 payors can draw on a range of expertise in multiple disciplines that allows them to critically 110 evaluate information presented to them by firms, including an evaluation of the limitations and 111 reliability of that information. FDA recognizes the value of payors receiving truthful and not 112 misleading information about unapproved medical products and unapproved uses of 113 approved/cleared medical products, as described in section 502(gg) of the FD&C Act, in order to 114 inform their decision-making. 115

Because Congress sought to address the use of HCEI in the context of these promotional materials, and firms have disseminated this information through promotional labeling materials, FDA’s longstanding approach has been to consider communication of HCEI about drugs under this section to be promotional labeling. See also Q9. The Agency similarly considers communications of HCEI about devices to be promotional labeling.

candidates.statement: Section 502(a) states that HCEI shall not be considered false or misleading if, among other 238 things, it is “based on competent and reliable scientific evidence.” FDA considers HCEI to be 239 based on CARSE if the HCEI has been developed using generally accepted scientific standards 240 that are appropriate for the information being conveyed and that yield accurate, reliable results. 241 In evaluating whether the amount and type of evidence that forms the basis for a particular 242 communication of HCEI meets the generally accepted scientific standards for such information, 243 FDA will consider existing current good research practices for substantiation developed by 244 authoritative bodies. Examples of such bodies include but are not limited to the International 245 Society for Pharmacoeconomic and Outcomes Research (ISPOR), the International Society for 246 Pharmacoepidemiology (ISPE), the Patient-Centered Outcomes Research Institute (PCORI), and 247 the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality (AHRQ). For example, when evaluating HCEI 248 based on indirect treatment comparisons in the absence of data from head-to-head controlled 249 clinical trials, FDA may refer to guidelines issued by external expert bodies regarding current 250 rigorous methodologies and best practices for such comparisons (e.g., network meta-analyses). 251

candidates.statement: Under section 502(a), HCEI includes the “clinical data, inputs, clinical or other assumptions, 260 methods, results, and other components underlying or comprising the analysis” of a medical 261 product’s economic consequences. FDA considers the CARSE standard in section 502(a) to 262 apply to all components of HCEI, including inputs and assumptions related to both economic 263 consequences and clinical outcomes (i.e., safety and/or effectiveness). As discussed previously 264 in Q4, such information must also relate to an approved indication in order to fall within the 265 provisions of section 502(a) regarding HCEI. 266

For example, if a particular HCEI presentation is based on real-world data where 382 actual patient use of a medical product falls outside of the recommended dosing/use regimen in 383 the FDA-approved labeling, the firm could include a statement such as “The dosing regimen 384 used in this study varies from the dosing regimen in the FDA-approved labeling,” in conjunction 385 with the HCEI presentation and in a font size comparable to that used for the other information 386 in the presentation. This example is not intended to suggest this is the only way for this 387 information to be presented.
